```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", cache.lazy = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(RIQITE)
set.seed(1)
nperm = 1000
```

This vignette illustrates using the RIQITE package by implementing the analyses shown in the main paper (Li and Miratrix). It mirrors `demo_code/RIllustration20221028.Rmd`, adapted to build as a package vignette: the illustrative instrumental-variable dataset ships with the package as `birth_school_age` rather than being hand-rolled inline, `setwd()` and `save.image()` calls have been removed, and a few simulation sizes have been reduced so the vignette builds in a reasonable amount of time (the main paper uses larger permutation and simulation counts for publication-quality precision).

# Testing monotonicity of an instrumental variable

We use `birth_school_age`, data constructed to match the summary statistics reported in Black et al. (2011) -- Table 1 cross-tabulates month of birth and school entry age (early/on-time/late), and Table 3 reports the total number of subjects born in January or December (the "discontinuity subsample"): 104,023, rounded here to 104,000, split evenly between the two birth months following Fiorini and Stevens (2014). See `?birth_school_age` for details; this is a reconstruction from published aggregate proportions, not a set of real individual records.

```{r get_the_data}
data(birth_school_age)
dat <- birth_school_age
table(dat$BirthMonth, dat$EntryTiming)
```

The following figure shows the empirical distribution functions of the school-entry age of December-born and January-born subjects. From the figure, most children started school at an older age if they were born in January rather than December.

```{r entry_age_ecdf, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 3, fig.align = "center"}
ggplot(dat, aes(EntryAge, color = BirthMonth, linetype = BirthMonth)) +
  stat_ecdf(geom = "step", show.legend = FALSE, linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("text", x = c(7.2, 7.2), y = c(.145, .81),
           label = c("January", "December")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(6, 8, .2)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.background = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = .5)) +
  labs(x = "School-Entry Age (Years)", y = "Probability")
```

We first perform the standard regression analysis assessing the relation between the instrument (birthday) and the school-entry age.

```{r F_test}
lm.fit <- lm(EntryAge ~ (BirthMonth == "Dec"), dat)
cat(paste(
  "estimated average effect is", round(as.numeric(lm.fit$coefficients[2]), digits = 3),
  "and F statistic is", round(as.numeric(summary(lm.fit)$fstatistic[1]), digits = 0),
  "\n"
))
```

This would conventionally be considered persuasive evidence of a valid instrument. We then perform the randomization test for the bounded null $H_{\le 0}$ on the monotonicity of the instrument: the difference-in-means statistic, the Wilcoxon rank sum statistic, and the Stephenson rank sum statistic with parameter $s = 10$, along with the classical Student's $t$-test, producing Table 1 in the paper.

```{r p_value_for_bounded_null, cache=TRUE}
dat$Z = as.numeric(dat$BirthMonth == "Dec")
dat$Y = dat$EntryAge
n <- length(dat$Z)
m <- sum(dat$Z)
# NOTE: the main paper uses nperm = 10^4; reduced here so the permutation
# matrix (n x nperm) stays small enough to build quickly and with modest
# memory in a vignette.
nperm <- 10^3

Z.perm <- assign_CRE(n, m, nperm)

# difference-in-means
pval.dim <- pval_bound(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, c = 0, method.list = list(name = "DIM"),
                        alternative = "greater", Z.perm = Z.perm, impute = "control")
ci.dim <- ci_bound(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, alternative = "greater", method.list = list(name = "DIM"),
                    Z.perm = Z.perm, impute = "control", alpha = 0.10)

# Wilcoxon rank sum (Stephenson with s = 2)
pval.wilc <- pval_quantile(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, k = n, c = 0, alternative = "greater",
                            method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 2), Z.perm = Z.perm)
ci.wilc <- ci_quantile(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, k.vec = n, alternative = "greater",
                        method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 2), Z.perm = Z.perm, alpha = 0.10)

# Stephenson rank sum, s = 10
pval.steph10 <- pval_quantile(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, k = n, c = 0, alternative = "greater",
                               method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 10), Z.perm = Z.perm)
ci.steph10 <- ci_quantile(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, k.vec = n, alternative = "greater",
                           method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 10), Z.perm = Z.perm, alpha = 0.10)

# classical Student's t-test
ttest = t.test(dat$Y[dat$Z == 1], dat$Y[dat$Z == 0], alternative = "greater")
pval.ttest = ttest$p.value
ci.ttest = round(ttest$conf.int[1], digits = 3)

result = data.frame(test = c("diff-in-means", "Wilcoxon", "Stephenson 10", "t test"),
                     pval = c(pval.dim, pval.wilc, pval.steph10, pval.ttest),
                     lower = c(ci.dim, ci.wilc$lower, ci.steph10$lower, ci.ttest))
knitr::kable(result)
```

Finally, we infer the effect range. The range of the effect of birth month on school-entry age is at least a year, indicating significant individual effect heterogeneity.

```{r effect_range}
tau.max.lower = ci_quantile(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, k.vec = n, alternative = "greater",
                             method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 10), Z.perm = Z.perm, alpha = 0.05)$lower
tau.min.upper = ci_quantile(Z = dat$Z, Y = dat$Y, k.vec = 1, alternative = "less",
                             method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 10), Z.perm = Z.perm, alpha = 0.05)$upper
print(paste("lower confidence limit for effect range is",
            max(0, tau.max.lower - tau.min.upper)))
```

# Evaluating the effectiveness of professional development

We next evaluate a teacher professional development RCT where treated teachers were given a professional development course on electric circuits, from Heller et al. (2012). The cleaned data ships with the package.

```{r get_the_professional_development_data}
data(electric_teachers)

mod <- lm(gain ~ TxAny, data = electric_teachers)
est_ATE <- round(mod$coefficients[2], digits = 2)
est_ATE
```

```{r electric_teacher_histograms, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 3.2, fig.align = "center"}
hist(electric_teachers$gain[electric_teachers$TxAny == 1],
     xlim = range(electric_teachers$gain), freq = FALSE, ylim = c(0, 0.065),
     col = "grey", border = FALSE, breaks = 20,
     main = NULL, xlab = "gain score")
hist(electric_teachers$gain[electric_teachers$TxAny == 0],
     freq = FALSE, add = TRUE, breaks = 20, col = NULL)
```

We standardize gain by the control-side variation in outcome at baseline, to compare treatment and control variation in effect size units:

```{r standardize_outcomes}
sd_0 = sd(electric_teachers$Per.1[electric_teachers$TxAny == 0])
electric_teachers$std_gain = electric_teachers$gain / sd_0
electric_teachers %>% group_by(TxAny) %>%
  summarise(raw_mean = mean(gain),
            mean = mean(std_gain),
            var = var(std_gain),
            max = max(std_gain),
            min = min(std_gain),
            raw_sd = sd(gain),
            sd = sd(std_gain))
```

If there were no correlation between $Y_i(0)$ and $\tau_i$, the standard deviation of the treatment impacts would be, using $var(Y_i(1)) = var(Y_i(0)) + var(\tau_i)$, around $0.28\sigma$ in effect size units (the group standard deviations above are approximately 0.852 and 0.806):

```{r}
tx_het <- sqrt(0.852^2 - 0.806^2)
tx_het
```

## Determining an s-value for the test statistic

We plan on using a Stephenson's Rank Sum test, but need to determine an appropriate value of $s$. We first conduct a sensitivity analysis across a range of scenarios to determine which $s$ have the highest amount of power for the top 10 quantiles, the next 20 quantiles, and the next 40 quantiles.

To illustrate this process, we first run a check on what the best $s$ is for a single scenario, using the empirical distribution of control outcomes and a normally-distributed, uncorrelated treatment effect (in standardized units).

```{r run_single_s_explore, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(303020)
cdat = filter(electric_teachers, TxAny == 0)
ate = est_ATE / sd_0
# NOTE: the main paper uses R = 1000 replicates; reduced here to keep the
# vignette build time reasonable. Increase R for publication-quality
# precision.
R = 50
nperm = 10^3
s_list = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20)
res <- explore_stephenson_s(s = s_list,
                             n = nrow(electric_teachers),
                             Y0_distribution = cdat$std_gain,
                             tx_function = "rnorm", ATE = ate,
                             tx_scale = tx_het, rho = 0,
                             nperm = nperm,
                             R = R, calc_ICC = FALSE,
                             targeted_power = FALSE, k.vec = (233 - 99):233)
```

We get one row per targeted quantile and explored $s$, telling us how easy it was to detect effects at that quantile. Here is our performance on the 170th largest effect (of 233 effects):

```{r}
filter(res, k == 170)
```

We next make a grid of different scenarios to explore to see if our trends of best $s$ are consistent across different possible scenarios. This is the same grid of scenarios used in the paper; the simulation results are shipped alongside this vignette (`heller_s_check_results.rds`) so the vignette does not need to re-run the full multi-scenario simulation (which is considerably more expensive than the single-scenario check above) every time it is built.

```{r build_scenario_grid}
checks = expand_grid(TxVar = c(0.25, 0.75),
                      tx_dist = c("rexp", "rnorm"),
                      rho = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5))
# There is no treatment variation, nor correlation with Y0, when
# the tx impact is a constant.
checks = bind_rows(checks,
                    tibble(TxVar = 0, tx_dist = "constant", rho = 0))
```

```{r run_or_load_scenario_grid, include=FALSE}
cache_file = "heller_s_check_results.rds"
if (!file.exists(cache_file)) {
  checks$data = pmap(checks, function(TxVar, tx_dist, rho) {
    explore_stephenson_s(s = s_list,
                          n = nrow(electric_teachers),
                          Y0_distribution = cdat$std_gain,
                          tx_function = tx_dist,
                          nperm = nperm,
                          ATE = ate, tx_scale = TxVar, rho = rho,
                          R = R, calc_ICC = FALSE,
                          targeted_power = FALSE, k.vec = (233 - 99):233)
  })
  s_selector = unnest(checks, cols = "data")
} else {
  s_selector = readRDS(cache_file)
}
```

We aggregate our findings and see what $s$ provides the tightest confidence intervals across a range of quantile groups: the top 10, next 20, next 30, and next 40. For each group, we take the median of the median lower confidence bound. High points on the curve below indicate those $s$ that are more informative:

```{r plot_s_selector, warning=FALSE}
n_units = nrow(electric_teachers)
s_selector = mutate(s_selector,
                     group = cut(k,
                                 breaks = c(0, 233 - 60, 233 - 30, 233 - 10, 233),
                                 labels = c("v low", "low", "med", "high")))

s_selector$rho.f = factor(s_selector$rho,
                           levels = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5),
                           labels = c("rho = -0.5", "rho = 0", "rho = 0.5"))

avg = s_selector %>%
  group_by(s, group, rho, rho.f) %>%
  summarise(q_ci = median(q_ci), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(group != "v low")

s_agg = s_selector %>%
  group_by(s, group, rho, rho.f, tx_dist) %>%
  summarise(q_ci = median(q_ci), .groups = "drop")

s_agg %>%
  filter(group != "v low") %>%
  ggplot(aes(s, q_ci)) +
  facet_grid(rho.f ~ group) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_line(aes(col = tx_dist), linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "s", y = "Median lower CI bound", col = "Tx distribution:") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = unique(s_selector$s)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  geom_point(data = avg, col = "black", size = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.5, 2)) +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(1, "cm"),
        panel.border = element_rect(colour = "grey", fill = NA, linewidth = 1))
```

We can also tally up the winning $s$ across each of the 100 quantiles we are exploring:

```{r}
qis <- s_selector %>%
  group_by(TxVar, tx_dist, rho, group, k) %>%
  filter(q_ci == max(q_ci))
table(group = qis$group, s = qis$s, rho = qis$rho)
```

Looking across our results, a wide range of $s$ could be argued for; small $s$ costs us on the lower quantiles, and very large $s$ costs us across the simulations. We adjust our $s$ to try and optimize multiple goals at once, using, e.g., $s = 6$.

## Analyzing the teacher professional development data

With our selected $s = 6$ in hand, we first test the bounded null hypothesis that all individual effects are non-positive.

```{r heller_ptest, cache=TRUE}
selected_s = 6
nperm = 10^6
n_units = nrow(electric_teachers)
pval.steph <- pval_quantile(Z = electric_teachers$TxAny, Y = electric_teachers$gain,
                             k = n_units, c = 0, alternative = "greater",
                             method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = selected_s), nperm = nperm)
pval.steph
```

We then conduct inference for all quantiles of individual treatment effects, using Stephenson rank statistics with $s =$ `r selected_s` and $s = 2$ (i.e., Wilcoxon rank).

```{r heller_quantiles, cache=TRUE}
ci6 = ci_quantile(Z = electric_teachers$TxAny, Y = electric_teachers$gain, alternative = "greater",
                   method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = selected_s), nperm = nperm, alpha = 0.10)
ci6
```

```{r}
summary(ci6, c = c(-0.0001, 0, 6), k = c(140, 141, 145, 146, 164, 165, 233))
```

Comparing to Wilcoxon:

```{r heller_quantiles_wilcoxon, cache=TRUE}
ci2 = ci_quantile(Z = electric_teachers$TxAny, Y = electric_teachers$gain, alternative = "greater",
                   method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 2), nperm = nperm, alpha = 0.10)
summary(ci2, c = c(0, 6))
```

We can also visualize the bounds:

```{r heller_ci_plots, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6.4, fig.align = "center"}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
s_title = glue::glue("s={selected_s}")
plot_quantile_CIs(ci6, k_start = 102, main = s_title)
plot_quantile_CIs(ci2, k_start = 102, main = "s=2")
```

Finally, we infer the effect range by conducting two tests, one for greater and one for less.

```{r heller_hettx_test, cache=TRUE}
tau.max.lower = ci_quantile(Z = electric_teachers$TxAny, Y = electric_teachers$gain, k.vec = n_units,
                             alternative = "greater", method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = selected_s),
                             nperm = nperm, alpha = 0.05)$lower
tau.min.upper = ci_quantile(Z = electric_teachers$TxAny, Y = electric_teachers$gain, k.vec = 1,
                             alternative = "less", method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = selected_s),
                             nperm = nperm, alpha = 0.05)$upper
max(0, tau.max.lower - tau.min.upper)
```

In this case, we have no evidence of effect heterogeneity (all the effects could be the same).

# Evaluating the effects of six-month nutrition therapy

The main paper also analyzes a homefood nutrition-therapy trial (details at <https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03995303>, data at <https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/38X3LX>) the same way as the professional-development data above. That trial's raw data is third-party and not distributed with this package, so it is not reproduced in this vignette; see `demo_code/RIllustration20221028.Rmd` in the package source repository for the full analysis, which runs for anyone who downloads the data from the link above into `demo_code/data_store/`.
